source: Owner's brief for Finance Den / Crash Files Ep. 2 (2008 financial crisis), narration as supplied

sections.title: 15 September 2008
paragraphs: On Monday, the 15th of September 2008, a bank that had survived 158 years, two world wars and the Great Depression filed for bankruptcy. Lehman Brothers owed 619 billion dollars. It was, and still is, the biggest bankruptcy in American history.
That same day, the Dow Jones fell more than 500 points. Within a year, millions of people had lost their jobs, their savings and their homes. Not just in America, but around the world.
And the strangest part? It all started with something ordinary. A house. Millions of ordinary houses, bought with money that was never really there.
So how does a house break the world? I'm Liam, welcome to the Den. This is Crash Files, and today we're opening the biggest file of our lifetime.

sections.title: Cheap money, risky loans
paragraphs: Let's go back to the early 2000s. Interest rates in America were low, borrowing was cheap, and owning a home was the dream everyone was chasing.

Banks were happy to help. Maybe a little too happy. Lenders started giving mortgages to people who, honestly, were never going to be able to pay them back. People with weak credit. People with no proof of income. Some loans came with tiny payments for the first two years, then jumped once the teaser period ended.
These were called subprime mortgages. Risky loans to risky borrowers.
Now, you'd think a bank would be scared to lend like that. But here's the trick: most of these lenders didn't plan to keep the loans. They planned to sell them.

sections.title: The Wall Street machine
paragraphs: This is where Wall Street comes in.

Imagine thousands of mortgages poured into one big pot. Good ones, bad ones, all mixed together. Wall Street banks took that pot and turned it into bonds called mortgage-backed securities. Every month, the homeowners' payments flowed through the pot to whoever owned the bonds.

Then they went further. They sliced those bonds into layers, mixed them again, and created even more complicated products, called CDOs. The top layers were supposed to be the safest, because they'd get paid first.
And the ratings agencies, the companies paid to judge how risky these products were, stamped many of them AAA. The highest grade. As safe as government debt.
So a risky loan on a house in Nevada could end up, a few steps later, as a "safe" investment owned by a pension fund in Norway, a bank in Germany or an insurer in Asia.
The whole machine rested on one belief: house prices don't fall. Not nationally. Not all at once.

sections.title: Borrowed to the hilt
paragraphs: And the banks didn't just buy this stuff. They borrowed to buy it.

Take Lehman Brothers. In 2008, it held about 680 billion dollars of assets, supported by only 22.5 billion dollars of its own capital. By 2007, it was borrowing about 31 dollars for every 1 dollar it actually owned.
Let that sink in. When you're that leveraged, you don't need a disaster to go bust. If the things you own fall by just over 3%, your own money is gone. Completely.
It's like buying a house with almost no deposit. Great when prices rise. Deadly when they don't.

sections.title: Then prices fell
paragraphs: And then, they didn't.
From the middle of 2006, American house prices started falling. By mid-2009 they were down about 30% on average.
Those teaser loans reset to higher payments. Borrowers couldn't pay. Homes went into foreclosure. And the money flowing through all those mortgage bonds started drying up.
Suddenly, nobody knew what these AAA products were really worth. And when nobody knows what something is worth, nobody wants to buy it, and nobody wants to lend against it.

The first big domino fell in March 2008. Bear Stearns, one of Wall Street's major investment banks, ran out of cash. On the 16th of March, JPMorgan bought it for 2 dollars a share. Just days earlier, it had been trading around 30.
That was the warning. Most people didn't listen.

sections.title: September 2008
paragraphs: Then came September. And September moved fast.
On the 7th, the US government took over Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the two giants that stood behind a huge part of America's mortgages.
On the 15th, Lehman Brothers collapsed. This time, there was no rescue. The government let it fail.
On the 16th, just one day later, the government did rescue AIG, the insurance giant that had sold protection on many of these mortgage products. The price: 85 billion dollars, for 80% of the company.
Banks stopped trusting each other. Lending froze. Companies couldn't get the short-term loans they needed to pay workers.

On the 3rd of October, Congress approved a 700 billion dollar rescue fund, called TARP. And the Federal Reserve cut interest rates from 5.25% all the way down to almost zero, then started buying assets on a scale nobody had seen before: about 1.75 trillion dollars.
The system didn't collapse completely. But the damage was already done.

sections.title: The damage
paragraphs: The American stock market, measured by the S&P 500, fell 57% from its peak in October 2007 to the bottom in March 2009.
The recession ran from December 2007 to June 2009. Eighteen months. The longest since World War Two. The economy shrank by 4.3%, the biggest drop since the war.
Unemployment doubled, from 5% to a peak of 10%. American households saw their net worth fall from about 69 trillion dollars to 55 trillion.
And about four million families lost their homes to foreclosure.
The homes that started the whole story ended it too.

sections.title: Three lessons
paragraphs: So what's the lesson?

When the official US inquiry finished its investigation in 2011, its conclusion was blunt. The crisis, it said, was "the result of human action and inaction." Warning signs were there. And the regulators, in its words, were not at their posts.
I see three lessons.
One: leverage turns small problems into fatal ones. Borrowing 31 to 1 means you can't afford to be even a little bit wrong.
Two: when everyone says something can't fall, be careful. House prices could fall. They did.
And three, the same lesson we saw in Singapore: rules only work if someone is actually checking.

sections.title: How a house broke the world
paragraphs: So, how does a house break the world? When millions of risky loans get dressed up as safe ones, sold around the planet, and bought with borrowed money, all it takes is for house prices to stop rising.
That's 2008.

Next time in Crash Files, we go back to the day markets fell 22% in a single day: Black Monday, 1987. If you want to understand how money really works, and how it breaks, subscribe, and I'll see you in the Den.
This video is for education only, not financial advice.
